passages.happening:
Thirteen years have passed since Ishmael was born. Abram is ninety-nine. The LORD appears and says, “I am God Almighty. Walk before Me and be blameless” (verse 1). He promises to make his covenant with Abram and to multiply him greatly (verse 2).

Abram falls on his face (verse 3). God says, “You will be the father of many nations” (verse 4), and gives him a new name: “No longer will you be called Abram, but your name will be Abraham, for I have made you a father of many nations” (verse 5).

Kings will come from him (verse 6). The covenant will be “an everlasting covenant” with his descendants, “to be your God and the God of your descendants after you” (verse 7). And God promises them “all the land of Canaan” (verse 8).
passages.hearers:
‘God Almighty’ is in Hebrew El Shaddai. It is the name God uses in Genesis when he makes promises of children and families (see 28:3 and 35:11). Its exact meaning is not certain, but it was heard as a name of power.

‘Walk before Me and be blameless’ does not mean ‘never make a mistake’. It means live your whole life in God's sight, with an undivided heart.

In the ancient world a name stood for who you were. When a greater person renamed someone, it showed that he had a claim on them. Pharaoh later renames Joseph (41:45), and a Babylonian official renames Daniel (Daniel 1:7). Here God renames Abram.

Abram is usually understood to mean ‘exalted father’. The new name, Abraham, is explained by a play on words: it sounds like the Hebrew for ‘father of a multitude’. God renames him before the child is even born. The name is a promise.

The heart of the covenant is in verse 7: ‘to be your God’. More than land or children, God promises himself.
passages.later:
Paul quotes verse 5: “I have made you a father of many nations” (Romans 4:17). He says Abraham believed “the God who gives life to the dead and calls into being what does not yet exist” (Romans 4:17). Through faith in Christ, people from many nations become Abraham's children.

The promise ‘I will be their God’ runs through the whole Bible. Jeremiah's new covenant says, “I will be their God, and they will be My people” (Jeremiah 31:33). And at the very end the Bible says it again about the new creation (Revelation 21:3).

The promise of kings leads to David, and the Gospels trace Jesus' family through David back to Abraham (Matthew 1:1).
passages.asks: God gave Abraham a new name before anything in his life looked different. Ask what name you give yourself: failure, too old, too late, not enough. Then ask what God says about you, and whether you will let his word name you.

passages.happening:
God gives Abraham a sign of the covenant. “Every male among you must be circumcised” (verse 10). Circumcision means cutting off the foreskin of the penis. It “will be a sign of the covenant between Me and you” (verse 11).

Baby boys are to be circumcised “when he is eight days old”, including those born in the household and those bought from foreigners (verse 12). “My covenant in your flesh will be an everlasting covenant” (verse 13).

Any male who is not circumcised “will be cut off from his people; he has broken My covenant” (verse 14).
passages.hearers:
Circumcision was not new. It was practiced in Egypt long before Abraham's family. A carved scene in a tomb at Saqqara in Egypt, from the 2300s BC, shows it being done. Jeremiah later names Egypt, Edom, Ammon and Moab among peoples who were circumcised (Jeremiah 9:25-26).

What was new was when it was done and what it meant. Among many peoples it seems to have marked growing up, as in the Egyptian scene, where it is done to a youth. In Abraham's family it was done to babies on the eighth day. It did not mark becoming a man. It marked belonging to God's covenant from the very beginning of life.

It was not only for blood relatives. Servants born in the house and those bought from foreigners received it too (verse 12). Belonging to Abraham's family was never only a matter of birth.

There is also a play on words. A covenant was ‘cut’ (15:10). The man who refuses the cut is ‘cut off’ from his people.

Jewish families still keep this sign today, on the eighth day, as a sign of the covenant with Abraham. Christians should speak of it with respect.
passages.later:
The Law of Moses keeps the eighth day (Leviticus 12:3). And from early on the Bible says the outward sign is meant to go deeper: “Circumcise your hearts, therefore, and stiffen your necks no more” (Deuteronomy 10:16). Moses promises, “The LORD your God will circumcise your hearts” (Deuteronomy 30:6).

Paul says the same: “circumcision is a matter of the heart, by the Spirit, not by the written code” (Romans 2:29). He points out that Abraham was counted righteous before he was circumcised, and that he received circumcision “as a seal of the righteousness that he had by faith” (Romans 4:11).

Jesus himself was circumcised on the eighth day (Luke 2:21). In the early church the great question was whether Gentile Christians had to be circumcised. The apostles said no (Acts 15). Paul writes, “in Christ Jesus neither circumcision nor uncircumcision has any value. All that matters is faith, expressed through love” (Galatians 5:6).
passages.hard:
Does circumcision given to babies mean that baptism should be given to babies? Christians have long answered this in different ways, and faithful churches stand on both sides.

Churches that baptize babies (among them Catholic, Orthodox, Lutheran, Anglican, Presbyterian and Reformed churches) point to this chapter. God gave the sign of his covenant to children who could not yet believe. Paul links circumcision and baptism (Colossians 2:11-12). Peter said, “This promise belongs to you and your children” (Acts 2:39), and whole households were baptized (Acts 16:15, 33).

Churches that baptize only those who profess faith (among them Baptist, many free churches and Pentecostal churches) point to what is new in the new covenant. Jeremiah promised that in it “they will all know Me” (Jeremiah 31:34). In the New Testament, baptism follows repentance and faith. And Paul's point in Romans 4 is that Abraham believed before he received the sign.

These notes take no side. Both agree that the covenant rests on God's promise, not on anything we have earned.

Nothing here is said against Jewish practice. Circumcision is a sign God gave Abraham's family, and Jewish families keep it to this day.
passages.asks: Circumcision was a sign in the body that you belonged to God. Paul says what God wants most is a changed heart. Ask whether your faith has only outward signs: a church, a habit, a label. Then ask whether God has your heart.

passages.happening:
God speaks about Sarai too: “do not call her Sarai, for her name is to be Sarah” (verse 15). “I will bless her and will surely give you a son by her” (verse 16). She will be the mother of nations, and kings will come from her (verse 16).

“Abraham fell facedown. Then he laughed” (verse 17). He says to himself, “Can a child be born to a man who is a hundred years old? Can Sarah give birth at the age of ninety?” (verse 17).

He says to God, “O that Ishmael might live under Your blessing!” (verse 18).

God answers that Sarah will bear a son, “and you are to name him Isaac” (verse 19). The covenant will go through Isaac. “As for Ishmael, I have heard you, and I will surely bless him” (verse 20). He will be the father of twelve rulers, and a great nation (verse 20). Isaac will be born “at this time next year” (verse 21).
passages.hearers:
Both Sarai and Sarah mean ‘princess’. The new name marks a new start rather than a new meaning. And for the first time God names Sarah in the promise. The son will not come through a servant or a plan. He will come through Sarah.

Abraham's laugh is the honest laugh of an old man. He bows down and laughs at the same time. It is hard to believe that a man of a hundred and a woman of ninety could have a baby.

The name Isaac means ‘he laughs’. God takes Abraham's laugh and puts it into the child's name. Every time they call their son, they will remember that they laughed, and that God kept his word.

Abraham loves Ishmael. He has raised him for thirteen years. His first prayer is for him. And God hears it. Ishmael's name means ‘God hears’, and here God says to Abraham, ‘I have heard you’.
passages.later:
God keeps his word to Ishmael. Genesis later lists his sons: “twelve princes of their tribes” (Genesis 25:16).

When Isaac is born, Sarah says, “God has made me laugh, and everyone who hears of this will laugh with me” (Genesis 21:6).

Hebrews says of Sarah that “she considered Him faithful who had promised” (Hebrews 11:11). Paul says Abraham faced the facts about his body, “since he was about a hundred years old” (Romans 4:19), and still trusted God.
passages.asks: Abraham laughed at God's promise, and God did not take it back. He put the laugh into the boy's name. Ask what promise of God you find hard to believe. Then bring that honest doubt to God, the way Abraham did, and see what he does with it.

passages.happening:
“On that very day Abraham took his son Ishmael and all those born in his household or purchased with his money” (verse 23), and he circumcises them, “just as God had told him” (verse 23).

Abraham is ninety-nine years old. Ishmael is thirteen (verses 24-25). “Abraham and his son Ishmael were circumcised on the same day” (verse 26), and every man in the household with them (verse 27).
passages.hearers:
Abraham laughed in verse 17. Now he obeys at once. Doubt and obedience sit side by side in the same chapter. He does not wait until he understands.

Ishmael is circumcised too. He is not the son of the covenant God will make with Isaac, but he is inside Abraham's household and bears its sign. God's blessing on him is real.

Ishmael's age, thirteen, was remembered. The Jewish historian Josephus, writing in the first century AD, said that the Arabs of his day circumcised their boys at thirteen because Ishmael had been circumcised at that age.

The whole household is included, servants born there and servants bought from outside. No one is left out of the sign.
passages.later:
Paul writes that Abraham received circumcision “as a seal of the righteousness that he had by faith while he was still uncircumcised” (Romans 4:11). The faith came first; the sign came after, and Abraham obeyed it.

James says the same kind of thing about Abraham's later obedience: “his faith was working with his actions” (James 2:22).
passages.asks: Abraham obeyed ‘on that very day’. Ask whether there is something you know God has asked of you that you keep putting off. What would it look like to do it today?
